questions.stem: A competent adult Jehovah's Witness refuses a life-saving transfusion after being fully informed. Which principle most directly requires the physician to respect this?
questions.explanation: A voluntary, informed, competent refusal must be respected, even for life-saving treatment (autonomy). A: Beneficence pulls toward transfusing. B: Overriding the refusal would be paternalism, which the lecture says is no longer the accepted norm. D: Justice concerns fair distribution. E: Utility is the consequentialist principle of the greatest good for the greatest number.

questions.stem: A resident believes she must disclose a colleague's missed lesion to the patient because lying is wrong regardless of consequences. Which theory is she applying?
questions.explanation: Deontology (Kant, duty-based): an act is right or wrong in itself under a rule, regardless of outcome; Kant's first formulation is to always tell patients the truth. B, D: These judge an act by its consequences. C: Virtue theory asks what a good person would do. E: Double effect concerns an act with an intended good effect and a foreseen, unintended harmful one.

questions.stem: Which Belmont Report principle is applied through fair selection of research subjects?
questions.explanation: Justice → fair subject selection. A: Respect for persons → informed consent. B: Beneficence → risk/benefit assessment. C, E: Not Belmont's three principles.

questions.stem: A hysterectomy for uterine cancer in a pregnant woman ends the pregnancy. Which reasoning justifies the surgery?
questions.explanation: The intended, good effect is saving her life; fetal death is foreseen but neither intended nor the means to the good effect. A: Weighing the greatest good for the greatest number is not the reasoning the lecture applies. C: She decides, so it isn't paternalism. D: Justice concerns fair distribution of resources. E: Virtue theory asks what a good person would do, not how to treat a harmful side effect.

questions.stem: Which set of criteria do standard (UNOS-style) organ-allocation ethics weigh?

options.A: Urgency, age, social role, time on the waiting list
options.B: Compatibility, social support, number of dependents, urgency
options.C: Likelihood of benefit, ability to pay, compatibility, waiting time
options.D: Lifestyle, urgency, compatibility, time on the waiting list
options.E: Urgency, compatibility, likelihood of benefit, time on the waiting list

questions.explanation: Medical urgency, compatibility, likelihood of benefit and waiting time are weighed; judgments of social worth, lifestyle or 'deservingness' are deliberately excluded. A: Social role is a social-worth judgment. B: Social support and dependents are social-worth judgments. C: Ability to pay is not a criterion. D: Lifestyle is excluded.

questions.stem: On the lecture's risk–benefit grid, how is an intervention with high risk and high benefit classified and handled?
questions.explanation: High risk with high benefit is 'hazardous', and the decision is the patient's. A: Futile is low risk, low benefit. B: Consented is low risk, high benefit. C: Unacceptable is high risk, low benefit. E: Letting the physician decide would be paternalism.

questions.stem: In which situation does the lecture describe paternalism as broadly accepted?

options.A: A competent Jehovah's Witness refusing a transfusion
options.B: An 88-year-old choosing watchful waiting for metastatic cancer
options.C: A patient who is an immediate danger to himself after a suicide attempt
options.D: A well-informed patient who disagrees with the physician's preferred option
options.E: A patient who asks that his HIV status be kept from his wife

questions.explanation: Justified paternalism: when a patient is a danger to themselves, beneficence requires intervening because the patient cannot, at that moment, act in their own best interest. A, B: Competent, informed refusals that autonomy requires respecting. D: The ideal physician respects the informed patient as a partner. E: A confidentiality question, not one of overriding the patient's own treatment choice.
